sec.label: I.
sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: In recent years, significant attention has been paid to autonomous driving systems, such as Autoware [1] which has emerged as an open-source software and is accelerating autonomous driving systems. Autonomous driving systems are currently mainly expected to be used in buses and taxis, and are attracting attention as an effective solution to social problems such as the shortage of drivers and transport in underpopulated areas. The internal design of autonomous driving systems is inherently complex, and in addition, high processing power, low power consumption, and strict real-time performance are required. A common approach to addressing this complexity is modeling with a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) [2], [3], [4]. DAG is particularly effective for representing processes and their dependencies, and various studies have explored their application in scheduling. In addition, there has been recent studies on DAG scheduling using machine learning [5], [6]. Furthermore, clustered many-core processors have attracted attention as an approach to high resource requirements and real-time constraints [7].

Clustered many-core processors, where cores are divided into groups called cluster and each has its own private memory, have been extensively studied for DAG scheduling or real-time applications because of their potential to mitigate memory contention [8], [9], [10], [11], [12], [13], [14], [15], [16]. By leveraging a large number of cores, these architectures can reduce clock frequency and power consumption while maintaining performance. Data sharing within a cluster is efficient via local shared memory, whereas inter-cluster communication, relying on NoC (Network on Chip) and DDR, involves higher latency. Consequently, while clustered many-core processors effectively reduce memory contention, they face latency issues due to inter-cluster communication.

Numerous studies have explored DAG scheduling for real-time systems using clustered many-core processors [8], [9], [10], [11], [17], [18]. However, relatively few studies have focused on minimizing inter-cluster communication. For instance, a previous study [19] introduces a static analysis-based algorithm to reduce inter-cluster communication between nodes with dependency relationships. However, this approach only addresses the cases where two dependent nodes allocate cores from different clusters. It does not consider scenarios in which a single node is assigned cores across multiple clusters, which can occur in high-load applications. Furthermore, the number of occurrences of inter-cluster communication may vary depending on cluster architectures, for example, the number of clusters and the number of total cores in processors. Various types of clustered many-core processors have recently emerged, such as P870-D [20], which is a RISC-V based clustered many-core processor, Kalray MPPA-256 [21], and Kalray MPPA3-80 [22]. However, to the best of our knowledge, there are no comprehensive studies investigating the impact of different cluster architectures and total core counts on inter-cluster communication in DAG scheduling.

This study models an autonomous driving system as a DAG and proposes a dynamic cluster selection method to reduce inter-cluster communication both within a node and between nodes. In contrast to existing approaches, the proposed method does not rely on features specific to any particular cluster architecture. This means that it can be adapted to various types of cluster architectures, regardless of the specific number of cores or clusters. Although this method is for a multi-rate DAG task with multiple periodic nodes, it can also be applied to a general single-rate DAG. In addition, the nature of dynamic cluster selection enables its application in systems with variable execution times. In this study, 12 different cluster architectures are examined by varying the number of clusters and total cores. The number of occurrences of inter-cluster communications within a node and between nodes is examined in each structure. Furthermore, response times are compared when the time of inter-cluster communication is varied.

The contributions of this paper are as follows: •
We propose a dynamic cluster selection method for DAG tasks that can reduce inter-cluster communication both within a node and between nodes.•
We show that the proposed method can be adapted to various cluster architectures by evaluating 12 different cluster architectures using two different task sets with respect to the number of required cores for each node.•
We show how inter-cluster communication within a node and between nodes affects response times by varying the time of inter-cluster communication.

The paper is organized as follows. Section II describes the target system and the platform used. Section III describes the proposed method. Section IV evaluates and discusses the scheduling results when using the proposed method. Section V describes related work. Section VI presents the conclusions.

sec.label: II.
sec.title: System Model
sec.p: This section provides an explanation of the assumed cluster architecture and the DAG structure.

sec.label: A.
sec.title: Architecture Model
sec.p:
The structure of the clustered many-core processor targeted in this study is described. The structure of the assumed clustered many-core processor is shown in Fig. 1. First, assume that the processor has $cluster\_num$ clusters and the number of all cores in the entire processor is $total\_core\_num$ . Each cluster has $\frac {total\_core\_num}{cluster\_num}(\geq 2)$ cores. Each cluster is given a private memory (SRAM) that can only be used by the cores in that cluster and is divided into memory banks for the number of cores in the cluster. In addition, NoC (Network on Chip) is assumed to be used for inter-cluster communication. For example, Kalray MPPA3-80 Coolidge [23] consists of 80 cores in five clusters, with NoC used for inter-cluster communication [10]. In this study, inter-cluster communication is assumed to be different clusters communicating via DDR. FIGURE 1.
Example of a structure of clustered many-core processors.

Cores within a cluster can share information using private memory, but cores belonging to different clusters each have to communicate with each other using NoC. Therefore, it is assumed that inter-cluster communication takes longer than intra-cluster communication in the processors assumed in this study. The inter-cluster communication overhead is included in the communication time between nodes in the DAG. The communication time is added to the execution time of the node receiving the data.

Measuring the actual communication overhead in a many-core processor environment is crucial. For this purpose, we used the Kalray Coolidge (MPPA3-80) processor. One illustrative method involves repeatedly measuring inter-cluster communication time while varying the data size. Inter-cluster communication, in this context, specifically refers to the process of copying data from one cluster to the DDR and subsequently copying that data from the DDR to another cluster. For our measurements, we assessed this two-step copy speed. Table 1 presents the average inter-cluster communication latency measured across varying data sizes: 1 B, 10 B, 1 kB, 10 kB, and 100 kB. For each data size, the communication was measured 1,000 times to obtain the average value. It is important to note that the minimum time interval measurable on the hardware used for this measurement is in microseconds. The data transfer operations between DDR and on-cluster memory are implemented using the standard C function memcpy, where the source and destination of the data are specified as arguments. The communication time for each complete transfer (from one cluster’s memory, through DDR, to another cluster’s memory) is determined by recording the timestamp before the initial memcpy call and after the completion of the final memcpy call using the C function clock_gettime, and then calculating the difference.TABLE 1Measured Inter-Cluster Communication Performance (Average Latency) between On-Cluster Memory and DDR on the Kalray Coolidge (MPPA3-80) Processor

Each cluster is equipped with a dedicated DMA controller responsible for all data transfers. These transfers include writing data from each cluster to the DDR and reading data from the DDR. For simplicity, it is assumed that the NoC structure is not complex and that the overhead of calculating the NoC routes for communication is negligible. Our dynamic cluster selection method can be adapted independently of the number of clusters and the number of cores in a cluster. However, architectures with complex NoC routes or communication environments will incur the overhead of finding appropriate communication routes, which will need to be addressed separately. As an example of communication on NoC, on the Kalray Coolidge (MPPA3-80) processor, NoC communication primarily uses wormhole switching with source routing, transmitting packets as 128-bit flits across two virtual channels.

sec.label: B.
sec.title: DAG
sec.p:
In an autonomous driving system, it consists of three parts: sensing, computation, and actuation [1], [4]. In the sensing part, inputs are received from sensors (e.g., LiDAR, camera, and GNSS) with different periods. In the computing part, the data received from the sensors is used for estimating self-position, path planning and object detection. In the actuation part, one vehicle control command is output for operations such as braking and steering wheel operation. This output is based on the processing results of the computing part. Therefore, this paper assumes a DAG with multiple periodic nodes at the entrance and one exit node. In fact, the DAG model is used to represent the workflow of such autonomous driving systems [2], [3], [4], [24]. The notation of DAG in this paper conforms to the study [2], [3]. Furthermore, a sample of the DAG used in this study is shown in Fig. 2. FIGURE 2.
Example of a simple DAG.

The DAG is represented by $G=(V,E)$ , where V and E are the set of vertices (nodes) and the set of directed edges, respectively. The nodes represent individual processes in the DAG, while the edges represent data flows and dependencies between nodes. V is represented as a set of $\tau $ with $n=|V|$ nodes, $V=\{\tau _{1}, \tau _{2}, \tau _{3}, \cdots , \tau _{i}, \cdots , \tau _{n}\}$ , where $\tau _{i}$ represents the $i^{th}$ node. An edge connecting two different nodes $\tau _{i}$ and $\tau _{j}$ is denoted as $e_{i, j} \in E$ . In this case, the data generated by $\tau _{i}$ is received by $\tau _{j}$ .

There are two types of nodes and edges, respectively. First, there are two types of nodes: timer-driven node and event-driven node. The differences between the two types of nodes are as follows: •
timer-driven node: a node that is triggered every given period, denoted by $\tau ^{td}_{i}$ .•
event-driven node: a node that is triggered when data from the immediately preceding node arrive, denoted by $\tau _{i}^{ed}$ .

Each timer-driven node $\tau _{i}^{td}$ has a period $T_{i}$ , and $T_{i} = T_{j}$ does not necessarily hold between $\tau _{i}^{td}$ and $\tau _{j}^{td}$ when $i \neq j$ . Secondly, there are two types of edges: triggered edges and update edges; the difference between the two types of edges is as follows: •
trigger edge: an event-driven node $\tau _{i}^{ed}$ is triggered when it receives data from this edge, denoted by $e^{tr}_{i,j}$ .•
update edge: a node is not triggered when it receives data from this edge. The data received is stored in a buffer and used for further processing after triggered, denoted by $e^{up}_{i,j}$ .

Note that the buffer that stores data from the update edge is overwritten each time new data arrive, and only the most recent data are stored. In Fig. 2, the timer-driven nodes are $\{\tau _{1}^{td}, \tau _{2}^{td}, \tau _{3}^{td}, \tau _{7}^{td}\}$ , the event-driven nodes are $\{\tau _{4}^{ed}, \tau _{5}^{ed}, \tau _{6}^{ed}, \tau _{8}^{ed}, \tau _{9}^{ed}\}$ , the trigger edges are $\{e^{tr}_{1,4}, e^{tr}_{2,5}, e^{tr}_{2,6}, e^{tr}_{7,8}, e^{tr}_{8,9}\}$ and the update edges are $\{e^{up}_{3,6}, e^{up}_{4,7}, e^{up}_{5,7}, e^{up}_{6,8}\}$ . The $\tau _{7}^{td}$ is activated in periods, but if new data have been received, the data is used by the update edge to process. This means that all timer-driven nodes do not have a trigger edge. This timer-driven node, which exists outside of the entrance, can be implemented for safety reasons. For example, in autonomous driving systems, many processes are interrupted in the end-to-end from the sensor at the entrance to the output, and there is a possibility that the process may be delayed significantly or stopped due to some problem in the middle of the process. In such cases, it will not be possible to produce a final output, and therefore, a stable output can be obtained by using the intermediate node as a timer-driven node that is triggered every given period and does not depend on the completion of the execution of the previous nodes.

Each node has the Worst-Case Execution Time (WCET) $C(\tau _{i})$ . Delays due to inter-cluster communication are not included in the WCET. Although it is pessimistic to treat the WCET of each node as a processing time when assuming a real system, the worst case is assumed to simplify the problem. The process that occurs at the $k^{th}$ activation of each node is called a job and is denoted as $\tau _{i,k}$ . The set of previous nodes connected by an edge to a node is denoted as $pred(\tau _{i})$ , and the set of immediate subsequent nodes connected by an edge is denoted as $succ(\tau _{i})$ . A sequence of $n (\geq 2)$ nodes on a DAG is called a path. Among them, the path with the largest sum of WCET of all nodes on the path and containing an entrance node and an exit node is called the critical path L.

In this study, each node has a parallel degree $K (0 \leq K \leq 0.9)$ . In other words, it is assumed that not only inter-node but also intra-node processing can be processed in parallel. This assumes that each node can use two or more cores for processing,1 if the value of K is not zero.1
Here, processes that can be computed in parallel within a node are assumed to have no data dependencies on each other (e.g., matrix multiplication).

If each node uses multiple cores for intra-node parallel processing, their execution times are updated by Amdahl’s law. Amdahl’s formula is given below.\begin{equation*} S(N) = \frac {1}{(1-K)+\frac {K}{N}} \tag {1}\end{equation*}

where $S(N)$ represents the ratio of speed-up when parallel processing with N cores, and K represents the degree of parallelism. For example, if the WCET of a node $\tau _{i}$ is $c_{i}$ , the new WCET $c_{new}(\tau _{i})$ when node $\tau _{i}$ is processed in parallel with N cores is $c_{new}(\tau _{i})=\frac {c_{i}}{S(N)}$ . sec.label: III.
sec.title: Proposed Method
sec.p:
This section presents an overview of the proposed method. The proposed method is based on dynamic scheduling, where each job dynamically selects the clusters at runtime. In this paper, we consider non-preemptive dynamic scheduling to simplify the cluster selection algorithm. The dynamic scheduling process is shown in Fig. 3. Scheduling continues until a defined end conditions are met, such as a specified time exceeded or the completion of a specific process. If these conditions are not met, all jobs that become available for execution are initially added to a priority queue. The number of required cores ($m^{req}_{i}$
) of the first job in the priority queue is then obtained. After that, if the number of cores remaining in all clusters ($sum(cluster\_remain\_cores)$
) is more than $m^{req}_{i}$
, it moves on to cluster selection for $\tau _{i}$
. Note that we assume non-preemptive scheduling.
FIGURE 3.
Flowchart of dynamic cluster selection, highlighting the proposed method.

The proposed method, detailed in Algorithm 1, is used in this cluster selection phase. The proposed method takes into account the effect of inter-cluster communication. Once clusters are selected, cores are allocated to meet the requirements of the job. This process is repeated until either the priority queue is empty or the number of required cores by the first job in the priority queue exceeds the total number of remaining cores. Cluster selection and core allocation are dynamically performed during job execution. If the priority queue is empty or there are not enough cores to meet a job requirement, it waits until the simulation unit time has passed and checks again whether the job is ready to run. The simulation unit time is the interval for periodically checking whether the job is ready to run. Note that the time to select a cluster of all executable jobs in the priority queue and allocate cores is significantly smaller than the simulation unit time. While waiting for an opening above the number of required cores by the first job in the priority queue, other jobs may be generated, and the head of the priority queue may be swapped. In such cases, the number of required cores by the first job is always evaluated first. In the proposed method, when a job is ready to run, clusters are selected considering the information about the node and the number of remaining cores in each cluster to reserve cores. This approach eliminates dependency on any specific cluster structure. Furthermore, although we assume in this study that the runtime of each node is WCET, the runtime information is not used in cluster selection and can therefore be used in systems with varying execution times. Algorithm 1
Cluster Selection Method

Data transfer between nodes is described. When a job that sends data on a trigger edge finishes processing, the job writes data to the DDR and leaves the written data in the all clusters it used at the same time. The job of the subsequent node is then started and, the cluster of the job is selected. If the subsequent job uses the same cluster as the one that is just used, the subsequent job can use the data left in the cluster, and the delay in writing to the DDR is negligible, or in other words, no inter-cluster communication occurs. Here, the writing to the DDR is performed by the DMA controller, and the cluster selection for the subsequent job is performed by the core that is previously used to process the job and has been released or other idle cores in the cluster. Therefore, writing to the DDR and cluster selection can be done in parallel, and that if the same cluster is selected, the data write time can be ignored. Jobs with only update edges do not store data in the cluster, but only write the DDR. Jobs read the required data from the DDR at runtime. For example, if the cluster used is different or if there is update data from the update edge, it reads the required data from the DDR. At this time, the time taken to read from the DDR is assumed to be negligible in the data transfer between nodes. In other words, inter-cluster communication is defined as a write delay to the DDR.

Here, the number of cores in each cluster that can be used to process nodes is $cluster\_core\_num =\frac {total\_core\_num}{cluster\_num}$ . The processing capacities of all cores are assumed to be equal. One of the idle cores is used to calculate the dynamic cluster selection. The information required for the proposed method (e.g., which cluster the job of the immediately preceding node is allocated to, and the number of cores remaining in each cluster) is collected from the DDR and retrieved from the DDR for each calculation. The time required to write and read the required information from the DDR is assumed to be negligible2 because these amounts of information can be assumed to be very small.2
In fact, the time to write from a core in the cluster to DDR and the time to read from DDR are measured on Kalray MPPA3-80 Coolidge. The data size of the communication is 100 bytes. In the same way, the time is measured by running a node with relatively short execution times in Autoware [1] on Kalray MPPA3-80 Coolidge. The results show that the communication time for reading and writing is at most $\frac {1}{200}$ of the node’s execution time.

sec.label: B.
sec.title: Algorithm Description
sec.p: From here, each line of Algorithm 1 is explained. Lines 1–3 deal with the case where the total number of remaining cores in each cluster is equal to $m^{req}_{i}$ . Here, clusters are selected using AIS (Ascending Index Selection). AIS is a simple cluster selection method used in the previous study [8], where the identification numbers (cluster index) assigned to each cluster in advance are reserved in descending order, starting with the smallest cluster index. In other words, the cluster with the smallest index is given the highest priority, and the cluster with the largest index is given the lowest priority. AIS selects clusters and returns the number of the selected clusters when the total number of remaining cores in the selected clusters is $m^{req}_{i}$ or more. Algorithm 1 uses AIS in selecting all available clusters, and there is no specific reason for this. The purpose of using AIS is simply to select all available clusters. AIS is used in Section IV as a comparison.

Lines 4–10 in Algorithm 1 are the cluster selection process when at least one or more clusters have more than the number of required cores $m^{req}_{i}$ remaining. In other words, only one cluster is selected. In Lines 5–7, clusters are selected using Pred_fit (Algorithm 2). Pred_fit is a method that checks whether cores can be secured from the same cluster as the job of previous node connected by the trigger edge ($pre\_tri\_node$ ) and selects the cluster if possible. First, the number of clusters most recently used by the job of $pre\_tri\_node$ is checked. If there is only one cluster used by the job of the $pre\_tri\_node$ , Pred_fit selects that cluster if it has a remainder greater than or equal to $m^{req}_{i}$ . This prevents inter-cluster communication between nodes. Note that timer-driven node does not have a trigger edge, and therefore, Pred_fit checks it on Line 2 in Algorithm 2. In Lines 8–10 in Algorithm 1, if the cluster could not be selected by Pred_fit, Best_fit (Algorithm 3) is used to select the cluster with the fewest remaining cores among clusters with $m^{req}_{i}$ or more remaining cores. The purpose of using Best_fit is to leave more cores in some clusters by using them from clusters with fewer cores.

Lines 11–19 are the cluster selection process when no cluster has more than $m^{req}_{i}$ remaining cores, but the total number of remaining cores in multiple clusters is more than $m^{req}_{i}$ . In other words, the process here is for securing multiple clusters. Here, the results of Greedy_fit (Algorithm 4) and Comb_fit (Algorithm 5) are compared to determine the clusters to be selected. Initially, the clusters are selected using Greedy_fit, which selects clusters in order with the cluster with the most remaining available cores and continues selecting clusters until the total number of remaining cores in the selected clusters reaches $m^{req}_{i}$ or more. When selecting multiple clusters that can secure $m^{req}_{i}$ cores, Greedy_fit is a method that can select the minimum number of clusters that satisfy the requirement. However, Greedy_fit is more likely to produce clusters with a small remainder of cores and cannot leave a large number of remaining cores in each cluster. Hence, when a job that requires a large number of cores subsequently arrives, it is likely to have to be handled by a large number of clusters. Therefore, the number of clusters secured by Greedy_fit is used as the number of elements for combination, and the combination of clusters in which the sum of the remaining cores of each cluster is $m^{req}_{i}$ is found using Comb_fit. Comb_fit is a method that searches for a combination of clusters with a given number of elements where the total remaining cores of $cluster\_remain\_cores$ is $m^{req}_{i}$ . Using Comb_fit makes it easier to leave many leftovers in some clusters, as the cluster with the largest remaining cores is not necessarily selected in contrast to Greedy_fit. For example, when the number of remaining cores in each of the three clusters is [A:2, B:7, C:8] and $m^{req}_{i}=10$ , Greedy_fit will select clusters in the order C $\rightarrow $ B. In this case, after core allocation, [A:2, B:5, C:0], inter-cluster communication occurs when the next job requires for six or seven cores arrives. However, if Comb_fit, A and B are selected and after core allocation [A:0, B:7, C:0]. Therefore, Comb_fit is more likely to suppress the occurrence of inter-cluster communication. The reason for not looking for pairs with a smaller number of clusters than that found by Greedy_fit is that the number of clusters found by Greedy_fit is minimal. If the return value from Comb_fit is not None, then use the combination of clusters found by Comb_fit (Lines 15–16 in Algorithm 1). If the return value is None, then use the combination found by Greedy_fit (Lines 17–18). An example of cluster selection in each step of Algorithm 1 is presented in Fig. 4. In Fig. 4, we assume that the $\tau _{c}$ job requires six cores. The status of the remaining cores in the cluster where each function is used, and the clusters actually selected are shown. FIGURE 4.
The following are specific examples of cases where each function is used in Algorithm 1. Example of the case where $\tau _{c}$ becomes executable after $\tau _{a}$ uses cluster 1. The number of clusters is assumed to be 5. AIS is used when $m^{req}_{c}$ equals the total number of cores remaining in all clusters. Pred_fit is used when there are more than $m^{req}_{c}$ cores remaining in cluster 1 used by $\tau _{a}$ . Best_fit is used when there are more than $m^{req}_{c}$ remaining in any cluster although Pred_fit could not be used. Clusters are selected by Comb_fit when it finds the same number of clusters as the number selected by Greedy_fit. If the number of clusters selected by Comb_fit is greater than the number of clusters selected by Greedy_fit, the clusters are selected by Greedy_fit.

Note that Algorithm 1 only selects a cluster to allocate cores. In actual scheduling, only $m^{req}_{i}$ cores are allocated from the cluster selected by Algorithm 1. In other words, the actual core allocation takes place after cluster selection. Thus, for example, if $m^{req}_{i}=7$ , even if two clusters (with 10 remaining cores in total) are selected, only seven cores are allocated. If multiple clusters are selected by Algorithm 1, they are allocated in order from the selected cluster until there are no more cores. This is because the order in which the clusters are selected is important, as the clusters are selected in order of the size of the remaining cores in Greedy_fit. Thus, if the proposed method chooses, for example, the clusters to be used in the order: cluster $3~\rightarrow $ cluster $1~\rightarrow $ cluster 2, the cores are allocated in this order.

sec.label: C.
sec.title: Computational Complexity
sec.p: Considering the computational complexity of Algorithm 1, the proposed method performs different processing based on three distinct scenarios, depending on the number of required cores and the available cores across clusters. In the first case, when the required cores exactly match the total of the remaining cores in each cluster, the algorithm employs the AIS strategy. Since AIS only selects clusters in sequential index order, if the number of clusters is set to n, the worst-case computational complexity is $O(n)$ .

In the second case, the algorithm applies the Pred_fit method. If this method fails to find a suitable cluster, it falls back to Best_fit. Pred_fit gets the immediately preceding node pre_tri_node that triggers the node $\tau _{i}$ to which a cluster is to be assigned, and then gets clusters in Line 5 that contain the core that was responsible for pre_tri_node. The process in Line 5 is a constant amount of time calculation by having pre_tri_node have the information of the corresponding clusters. Hence, Pred_fit has a constant computational complexity $O(1)$ . In contrast, Best_fit searches for the cluster with the minimum number of remaining cores that satisfies the required number of cores $m^{req}_{i}$ . This involves iterating through all clusters to determine the best candidate, which gives a per-iteration cost of $O(n)$ . Thereby, the computational complexity of Best_fit is $O(n^{2})$ , based on the computational complexity of the process of one loop and the number of loops. Here, it is possible to reduce the amount of computation by first looking for clusters that are greater than or equal to $m^{req}_{i}$ in Best_fit, and then selecting the smallest cluster. Combining Pred_fit and Best_fit, the worst-case complexity in the second case becomes $O(n^{2})$ .

In the third case, the algorithm invokes Greedy_fit followed by Comb_fit. Greedy_fit selects the cluster with the largest number of remaining cores from all the clusters and added to total_core, and the cluster search process ends when total_core is equal to or greater than the required number of cores $m^{req}_{i}$ . Since each argmax operation over all clusters takes $O(n)$ , and the loop is executed up to n times, the computational complexity of Greedy_fit is $O(n^{2})$ . On the other hand, Comb_fit then evaluates all combinations of r clusters (where r is the number identified by Greedy_fit) to find a set whose total available cores match $m^{rq}_{i}$ . The complexity of this step is $O\left ({{r \binom {n}{r}}}\right)$ , as it considers all such combinations. Thus, for the third case, the total computational complexity is $O\left ({{n^{2}+r \binom {n}{r}}}\right)$ . Therefore, the worst-case computational complexity of the proposed algorithm, Algorithm 1, is $O\left ({{n^{2}+r \binom {n}{r}}}\right)$ , from the computational complexity $O(n)$ , $O(n^{2})$ , and $O\left ({{n^{2}+ r \binom {n}{r}}}\right)$ for the three cases.

From this result, we can see that the worst-case computational complexity of Algorithm 1 is affected by n and r. The upper limit of n is $n \leq total\_core\_num$ within a realistic range. In addition, $0 \leq r \leq n$ . This makes it possible to estimate the worst-case computational complexity in more detail for each cluster architecture.

sec.label: IV.
sec.title: Evaluation
sec.p: Here, the proposed method is applied to DAG, and its performance is compared with those of other methods. The four methods compared are AIS (Ascending Index Selection), Best_fit, Greedy_fit, and WCM (WCRT-based Core allocation Method) [25]. These are used to determine which cluster to allocate the cores from.

sec.title: Basic Methods
sec.p:
AIS is the method used to select clusters in order of ascending cluster index. For example, if the indices of the five clusters are 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 respectively, then the cluster of 0 has the highest priority to be used and the cluster of 4 has the lowest priority. Best_fit and Greedy_fit are the methods introduced in Section III-B. Here, in Best_fit and Greedy_fit, if any cluster has more than the number of required cores, the cluster with the minimum and maximum number of cores is selected, respectively. On the other hand, if none of the clusters has more than the number of required cores, the cluster with the largest number of cores in each cluster is selected in order in Greedy_fit. Best_fit cannot be used in situations where cores are secured from multiple clusters, as it is only an effective method when there is a remainder of more than the number of required cores in any cluster. Therefore, for the purpose of comparison, we extend Best_fit. If no cluster has a remainder of more than the number of required cores, Best_fit uses Min_fit (Algorithm 6), which has the opposite property to Greedy_fit and selects successively from clusters with the smallest number of remaining cores. In other words, if the number of required cores can be handled by one cluster, the conventional Best_fit (Algorithm 3) is used, and if not, Min_fit (Algorithm 6) is used. Here, if the number of remaining cores in all clusters is greater than or equal to the number of required cores, Min_fit can be said to be the same concept as Best_fit. Note that Min_fit is only an algorithm for comparison and is not used in the proposed method. Best_fit to be compared will be a mixture of two algorithms, but for simplicity, the one that is a mixture of two also is denoted as Best_fit. Algorithm 6

sec.title: Existing Research
sec.p: WCM[25] is the latest core allocation method in DAG scheduling with many-core processors. WCM allocates cores to each node in two steps. In step 1, if the WCET in m cores of $\tau _{i}$ is $C^{m}_{i}$ and the period is $T_{i}$ , the minimum number of cores satisfying $C^{m}_{i} \leq T_{i}$ is calculated and assigned to $\tau _{i}$ . Here, a node that satisfies $C^{m}_{i} \leq T_{i}$ from the beginning is allocated one core. This is performed for all nodes.

In step 2, if there are extra cores in step 1, additional cores are allocated. In the additional allocation, the paths (including entrance and exit nodes) with the largest WCRT (Equation (13) in Ref [25]) are found, and to the node with the largest WCRT (Equation (1) in Ref [25]) among the path, one additional core is allocated. After one core is allocated, WCRT of that node is reduced, and the WCRT of the entire path is also reduced; therefore the path is searched again. The allocation is repeated until no cores are left. While the WCM assumes the system model with preemption, this paper assumes a non-preemptive system. Therefore, the equation used to calculate the WCRT of the nodes is modified from Equation (13) in Ref [25] as follows:\begin{equation*} R_{i} = C^{m_{i}}_{i}+B_{i} + \sum _{\tau _{j} \in hp(\tau _{i})} \left \lceil {{\frac {T_{i}}{T_{j}} }}\right \rceil \times C^{m_{j}}_{j} \tag {2}\end{equation*}

Here, $C^{m_{i}}_{i}$ represents the worst-case execution time when $\tau _{i}$ is executed in parallel using $m_{i}$ cores. The function $hp(\tau _{i})$ returns the set of nodes with higher priority than $\tau _{i}$ . Similarly, the function $lp(\tau _{i})$ returns the set of nodes with lower priority than $\tau _{i}$ . $B_{i}$ is the maximum time the process is blocked by a node with a lower priority than $\tau _{i}$ :\begin{equation*} B_{i} = \max \limits _{k \in lp(\tau _{i})} C^{m_{k}}_{k} \tag {3}\end{equation*} If a non-preemptive system is assumed, $B_{i}$ is added [26], as in Equation (2).

Since the WCM study assumes a generic non-clustered many-core system, the part of the system that actually allocates cores from which cluster is not proposed. In addition, WCM has disadvantages such as the tendency to over-accumulate cores on some nodes. Therefore, we evaluated inter-cluster communication by using WCM to determine the number of required cores by each node and by performing dynamic simulations. For the evaluation, we assessed WCM with the following four patterns by adding thresholds for cluster selection and the number of cores to be allocated. •
T-WCM: Cluster selection is done randomly. In addition, a threshold is set for the number of cores allocated to a single node.•
PT-WCM: Cluster selection is done by the proposed method (Algorithm 1), and the number of required cores for each node is determined by WCM. In addition, a threshold for the number of cores allocated to a single node is set.•
N-WCM: Cluster selection is done randomly. In addition, there is no threshold for the number of cores per node•
PN-WCM: Cluster selection is done by the proposed method (Algorithm 1) and the number of cores for each node is determined by WCM. There is no threshold for the number of cores allocated to a single node.

The clusters used in T-WCM and N-WCM are selected randomly, because the cluster selection part is not proposed in WCM. Clusters are selected at random, and this is done until the total number of remaining cores in the selected clusters exceeds the number of required cores of the node. This random selection is done in the highlighted part of the flowchart (Fig. 3). Since N-WCM does not set a threshold on the number of cores allocated to each node, it can be considered pure WCM. However, in all these four patterns, the maximum number of required cores by one node is set to $total\_core\_num$ . In this case, the number of required cores by each node is the same for PT-WCM and T-WCM. Similarly, PN-WCM and N-WCM have the same number of required cores by each node. In other words, the number of required cores by each node in each of these two pairs is different. This is because the number of cores allocated per node with and without the threshold is different.

In WCM, the number of available cores is equal to the total number of cores in the processor. This is because schedulability tests are performed after allocation to determine the schedule. In this study, the total number of cores allocated to each node is not necessarily the total number of cores in the processor, since the number of inter-cluster communication occurrences and their impact on response time are evaluated. However, the total number of required cores and the number of available cores for each node are the same among the methods being compared.

sec.title: Notations
sec.p: Here, when there are several clusters corresponding in each algorithm, for example, when there are several clusters with the same number of cores in Greedy_fit, the clusters with the smallest index are selected in order. These three methods are used instead of the proposed method in the comparative evaluation in the cluster selection part of the flowchart in Fig. 3, where there is a background color.

As mentioned at the end of Section III-B, the order of clusters for core allocation is important. Cluster selection in Greedy_fit, Best_fit, and AIS assumes that cores are allocated in the same order as in the proposed method, starting with the chosen cluster. Therefore, for example, if these methods choose the clusters to be used in the order: cluster $3~\rightarrow $ cluster $1~\rightarrow $ cluster 2, the cores are allocated in this order.

sec.title: Random DAG Generator
sec.p:
In this evaluation, 1,000 DAGs are generated for comparison using a random DAG generator. Five patterns are prepared for the number of nodes [40, 60, 80, 100, 120], each generating 200 DAGs. The number of entrance nodes of the generated DAG is randomly determined from [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] and the number of exit nodes is 1. The entrance nodes are also given random periods of [100 ms, 200 ms, 300 ms, 400 ms, 500 ms] respectively. RD-Gen [27] is used to generate DAG. This random DAG generator is available on Github, and RD-Gen can generate DAG in three different ways, and the Fan-in/Fan-out method is used to generate the DAG in this time. In RD-Gen, various parameters of the DAG can be set using a YAML file (sample_fan_in_fan_out.yaml is used in this case). For example, the number of edges where the node receives data (In-degree), the number of edges where the node sends data (Out-degree), and the execution time (Execution time) can be set. In this paper, this execution time is referred to as WCET. Note that the first WCET assigned is the value when executed on one core. In addition, deadlines can be generated by specifying the ratio of the length of the critical path of the DAG. The deadline is the length of the critical path multiplied by the specified ratio. These can be set in two ways: Random or Fixed. For example, Random: (1, 31, 2) means that the number of edges is set from 1 to 31 in increments of 2 (1, 3, 5, $\cdots $ , 31), will be determined at random. In addition, if Random: [1, 2, 3] is specified, one of the numbers 1, 2, or 3 is randomly selected. Furthermore, if Fixed: 20 is set, the value of the parameter is 20. These parameters will be common to all DAGs generated (if Random is used, the value chosen for each DAG will naturally be Random). Original parameters can also be added by creating a field called Additional properties in the YAML file. For more information on these parameters, check the original paper [27]. In this case, we have added the original parameters: parallelism K and Period. The period is also provided by default in the Chain-based method of RD-Gen. Details of the configured parameters are given in Table 4. In this evaluation, the number of timer-driven nodes other than the entrance is fixed to three for all DAGs; the three timer-driven nodes are selected from the non-entrance and non-exit nodes using the built-in Python function random(). sec.title: Assignment of Periods for Each Node
sec.p: To decide the trigger edge, a temporary period is allocated to the event-driven nodes other than the timer-driven nodes. Initially, the event-driven node following the timer-driven node is given the largest of the periods of the previous timer-driven node as its own period. The next event-driven node takes the largest of the periods of the previous event-driven node as its own period. If the previous nodes are an event-driven node and a timer-driven node, the largest period among them is used. For example, in Fig. 2, starting from $\tau ^{ed}_{4}, \tau ^{ed}_{5}, \tau ^{ed}_{6}$ , these provisional periods are $period(\tau ^{ed}_{4})=400$ , $period(\tau ^{ed}_{5})=200$ , $period(\tau ^{ed}_{6})=200$ , and $period(\tau ^{ed}_{8})=300$ , $period(\tau ^{ed}_{9})=300$ .

In this case, all edges to the timer-driven node are update edges, and if there is only one edge to the event-driven node, it is the trigger edge. If there are more than two edges to an event-driven node, the one from the node with the largest period is the trigger edge. If the periods of all the nodes behind are the same, the timer-driven node with the smallest node index is the trigger edge, and if they are all event-driven nodes, the one with the smaller node id assigned at the time of generation is the trigger edge.

sec.title: Scheduling Simulator Details
sec.p: This section describes the scheduling simulator in more detail. The simulator follows the flowchart in Fig. 3. The simulator initially reads a single DAG, and the HP (Hyper Period) of that DAG is obtained. HP is the least common multiple of the period that all timer-driven nodes have. The simulation then proceeded as one simulation time as one loop step, for a total of HP loop steps. If the job of the exit node had never finished at the end of the HP, the simulation continued until the job finished. Here, HP is assumed in ms, and one loop is treated as one ms. A single loop process consists of three main parts: dealing with jobs that have finished, creating new jobs and executing jobs in the priority queue. The decision from which clusters the cores are to be obtained is made before the job is executed. If the job executions are processed in parallel, a new WCET is obtained using Equation (1) in the same way as Section II-B, and if inter-cluster communication occurs, communication overhead is added to the WCET. Note that the inter-cluster communication time is added separately from the parallel execution time. If the WCET has a value of less than one ms (e.g., 23.5 ms), the value means that the process finished in the smallest integer loop above that value (i.e., the 24th loop).

Each job is given a priority by laxity [2]. laxity is calculated for each node from the deadline value given to the DAG. The smaller laxity, the less margin there is to the deadline, and the priority queue has the highest priority with the smallest laxity value. Since the job with the least number of activations has a higher priority, each job adjusted its priority by adding the value of $period \times (n-1)$ to laxity at the $n^{th}$ activation.
The simulation framework is written in Python (ver. 3.10.12) and runs on a system with 2.30 GHz 16-core Intel Core i7-11800H CPU, 32 GB RAM, and Ubuntu 22.04 LTS OS (64 bit).

sec.label: C.
sec.title: Preparation of Two Different Task Sets
sec.p: We created two types of task sets by varying the number of required cores by each node in the DAG: the average task set with 1–9 cores required by each node, and the heavy task set with $heavy\_task\_num$ heavy tasks require a very large number of cores. The number of required cores for the average task set is determined using random() in Python, and the number of required cores for each node did not change for each run or method using seed. Each heavy task requires $\frac {total\_core\_num}{heavy\_task\_num}$ cores, and other nodes require 1–3 cores. If $\frac {total\_core\_num}{heavy\_task\_num}$ has a remainder, the remainder is assigned to the $heavy\_task\_num$ tasks one by one in turn. The $heavy\_task\_num$ heavy tasks and the number of cores of other nodes are determined by random() with the seed set in the same way.

In the figures in Section IV that follow, Proposed, Greedy_fit, Best_fit, and AIS represent the results when the number of required cores is randomly determined in the average task set and heavy task set in the above random manner. PT-WCM and T-WCM are the evaluation results when the number of required cores is determined by WCM with a threshold of nine cores per node for the average task set and of $\frac {total\_core\_num}{heavy\_task\_num}$ cores per node for the heavy task set. The results are as follows. PN-WCM and N-WCM are the evaluation results when the number of cores is determined by WCM with no threshold. In one DAG, the number of required cores for each node is different when the number of required cores is determined randomly and when the number of required cores is determined by WCM. However, the total number of required cores is equal for all methods in a DAG. For example, suppose that in the average task set, the total number of required cores of all nodes of the DAG after randomly setting 1–9 cores is 100 (this includes the case of 1 core). If WCM is used, core allocation (strictly speaking, determination of the number of required cores) is performed until the total number of required cores for each node reaches 100. At this time, if there is a threshold, it is limited to 9 cores per core. The same can be considered for heavy task sets.

In the following sections, for simplicity, the method in which the number of required cores is determined randomly will be referred to as the Basic Methods. Based on the differences in the number of required cores by each node as described above, we will discuss each Basic Methods, PT-WCM and T-WCM, and PN-WCM and N-WCM, respectively, in the evaluation figures.

sec.label: D.
sec.title: Evaluation Metrics
sec.p: For both the average and heavy task sets, three indicators are evaluated: the number of inter-cluster communication occurrences within a node, between nodes, and the average maximum response time when varying the inter-cluster communication time.

Inter-cluster communication occurring within a node is assumed to occur when a node secures multiple cores from two or more clusters. For the sake of simplicity, we assume that if a node secures cores from n clusters, $n-1$ inter-cluster communications occur. This assumes that communication only occurs with neighboring clusters. For example, if a node secures six cores from three clusters, the number of inter-cluster communication occurrences is $3-1 = 2$ . For each DAG, the number of inter-cluster communication occurrences within a node is obtained, and the average of the number of occurrences in 200 DAGs with an equal number of nodes is calculated.

Inter-cluster communication that occurs between nodes is assumed to occur when the clusters used differ between jobs on two nodes linked by a trigger edge. More specifically, it is assumed that inter-cluster communication does not occur if the set of clusters (indices) used by the job sending the data is a subset of the cluster set used by the receiving job. For example, suppose there are nodes A and B and a trigger edge exists at $A~\rightarrow ~B$ . This will not occur if the cluster number used by A is (0, 2) and B is (0, 1, 2). Although node A does not use cluster 1 at this time, inter-cluster communication does not occur between nodes because data can be shared in clusters 0 and 2. However, inter-cluster communication within a node naturally occurs. Inter-cluster communication between nodes occurs when A is (0, 2) and B is (0, 1), as data needs to be sent from cluster 2 to cluster 0 or cluster 1. Since multiple clusters can write information from the cluster to the DDR at the same time, if inter-cluster communication occurs between nodes, the total number of inter-cluster communications between nodes is assumed to be once between them. Note that inter-cluster communication between nodes does not occur if a node has only update edges, because the data from the update edge is only read from the DDR, as described in Section III.

The response time of a DAG is determined based on the first timer-driven node found by following the trigger edges from the exit node. Whenever a job of the exit node finished, the response time is calculated by adding up the latest WCET and waiting time of each of jobs of nodes from the reference timer-driven node to the exit node by following the trigger edge. Each WCET included inter-cluster communication, while the waiting time is the time between each job being released (added to the priority queue) and its actual execution. Where, if inter-cluster communication occurred n times within a node, $n * cc\_cost$ is added to the execution time of the node as the inter-cluster communication time within that node. If inter-cluster communication occurred even once between a node and one previous node, $1 * cc\_cost$ is added to the execution time of that node as the inter-cluster communication time between nodes. The maximum response time in a single simulation is determined for each DAG, and the average maximum response time of 200 DAGs for each number of nodes is calculated. The change in average maximum response time when the value of $cc\_cost$ is varied from 0.1 to 5.0 in increments of 0.1 is investigated.

The results of the evaluation of inter-cluster communication within a node, between nodes, and average maximum response time in the average task set are discussed in Sections IV-E1, IV-E2, and IV-E3, respectively. Similarly, the results of the heavy task set are discussed in Sections IV-F1, IV-F2, and IV-F3.

sec.label: E.
sec.title: Evaluation of the Average Task Set
Comparison of Inter-Cluster Communication Within A Node in Fig. 5
sec.p:
A comparison of the number of occurrences of inter-cluster communication within a node in the average task set is shown in Fig. 5. If the rows are the same, the total number of cores used is the same; if the columns are the same, the number of clusters is the same pattern. Evaluations are carried out for a total of 12 patterns, with $cluster\_num$ being [5, 8, 10, 20] and $total\_core\_num$ being [80, 120, 160]. The same applies for all subsequent evaluations. FIGURE 5.
Comparison of the average number of inter-cluster occurrences within a node when the number of nodes is varied in average task set.

Analyzing the results for different methods reveals key insights. In the comparison between Best_fit and Greedy_fit, Best_fit performs better, especially when the number of clusters is small and the number of cores in a cluster is large. Best_fit minimizes inter-cluster communication by prioritizing the allocation of cores from clusters with fewer remaining cores, preserving cores in other clusters. In contrast, Greedy_fit selects clusters from a cluster with the most remaining cores, which balances core usage across clusters. Consequently, Greedy_fit encounters more situations requiring core allocation from multiple clusters compared to Best_fit. In scenarios with fewer clusters and larger cores per cluster, Best_fit maintains more cores in a single cluster, which is advantageous (in particular, (i) of Fig. 5).

On the other hand, overall, Greedy_fit reduces inter-cluster communication within a node better than Best_fit in other situations and especially when there are more jobs that can be processed in parallel. If the number of jobs that can be processed in parallel increases due to an increase in the number of nodes, each cluster is used for many jobs at once. As the number of parallel-processable jobs increases, the overall number of cores remaining in each cluster in the latter job execution phase decreases. Therefore, if a job in the second half requires many cores, a single cluster often cannot accommodate the demand, resulting in the selection of multiple clusters. In Best_fit, when the number of required cores exceeds the capacity of a single cluster, the Min_fit algorithm is used to select clusters with the minimum number of remaining cores in order. Therefore, when multiple clusters are required, Best_fit selects the maximum number of clusters. It can be seen that as the number of nodes increases, the results for the Best_fit and Greedy_fit are reversed ((j) and (k) of Fig. 5).

When securing cores from multiple clusters, Greedy_fit has a great advantage over Best_fit. Greedy_fit can secure the number of required cores with the minimum number of clusters in order. On the other hand, in Best_fit, the number of selected clusters is the largest. When the number of clusters is large, the number of required cores will increasingly exceed the number of remaining cores in each cluster, and Greedy_fit is considered to provide better results than Best_fit.

Overall, the proposed method is able to reduce inter-cluster communication within a node the most in Basic Methods. We believe that this is due to the appropriate use of Best_fit, Greedy_fit and Comb_fit in different situations. If the number of required cores can be handled by one cluster, Best_fit is basically used for remaining many cores in some clusters. Furthermore, if multiple clusters have to be selected, then Greedy_fit or Comb_fit is used to select the smallest number of clusters. This reduces the likelihood of inter-cluster communication occurring, while successfully minimizing the risk when inter-cluster communication does occur. Comb_fit is intended to fill the disadvantages of Greedy_fit. In Greedy_fit, the minimum number of clusters can be selected, but the maximum number of extra cores can be significantly reduced because the clusters are selected in the order with the most remaining cores. Comb_fit can select clusters remaining few cores and can select clusters with the same minimum number of elements as Greedy_fit, because it searches for combinations of clusters where the total number of required cores and the total number of remaining cores match.

AIS has the worst overall result. AIS selects from clusters with smaller indices unless the number of cores is zero. Therefore, even if there are more cores than required in a cluster and there are only a few cores in small-index clusters, the cluster with the smallest index will be selected first. Therefore, a situation arises where cores are secured from multiple clusters at a certain rate, regardless of the number of required cores or the number of cores remaining in each cluster. However, when the total number of cores is small and the number of clusters is very large ((d) of Fig. 5), Best_fit is even worse than AIS. This indicates that the disadvantage of Best_fit, which selects the largest number of clusters in situations where inter-cluster communication is expected to occur, has a greater impact than the disadvantage of AIS.

Next, a comparison of PT-WCM and T-WCM is discussed. These two have a threshold of nine cores per node, and Fig. 5 shows that PT-WCM significantly reduces inter-cluster communication within a node more than T-WCM. Compared to random selection, the proposed method shows that it is able to select to reduce inter-cluster communication. Comparing Proposed and PT-WCM, PT-WCM reduces inter-cluster communication more than Proposed. This is because WCM tends to bias cores toward some nodes when determining cores, resulting in an extreme increase in the number of nodes requiring nine cores and the number of nodes requiring only one core. Therefore, the number of nodes requiring multiple cores is reduced compared to the case of the Basic Methods, resulting in fewer inter-cluster communications overall.

Next, a comparison of PN-WCM and N-WCM shows that PN-WCM is slightly better. Without a threshold, WCM can allocate a large number of cores to a very few nodes in the worst case. This leads to the phenomenon that a very small number of nodes require cores close to the total number of cores, while almost all other nodes request only one core. As a result, the number of nodes requiring multiple cores is extremely small, and the difference is small.

The reason for excessive core allocation by WCM is that WCM allocates cores to the node with the largest WCRT value among the selected paths, as can be seen from Equation (2), the WCRT value is larger for nodes with lower priority. Since priority determination in this paper is done by laxity, the exit node has the lowest priority. Furthermore, since the exit node is included in all paths, it is the most likely to be selected for every assignment. This makes it extremely easy for cores to cluster at or near the exit node.

sec.title: Comparison of Inter-Cluster Communication Between Nodes in Fig. 6
sec.p:
Next, the average occurrence ratio of inter-cluster communication between nodes is shown in Fig. 6. Unlike Fig. 5, overall Best_fit has better results than Greedy_fit. Best_fit tends to concentrate jobs in some clusters because the clusters with the least remainder are used first. Therefore, Best_fit makes it difficult for jobs to be distributed to some clusters. Greedy_fit can be kept to a smaller number of clusters when cores are secured from multiple clusters. However, since the largest remaining cluster changes with each job execution, the clusters used by each job are much more distributed than in other methods. As a result, the clusters used by two jobs in a dependency relationship are rarely the same, resulting in many inter-cluster communications between nodes. FIGURE 6.
Comparison of the average number of inter-cluster occurrences between nodes when the number of nodes is varied in average task set.

Overall, it can be seen that the proposed method reduces inter-cluster communication between nodes the most. If the number of required cores by a job can be secured in one cluster, the proposed method firstly tries to select the cluster using Pred_fit. It thereby has a much higher chance of securing cores from the same cluster as the predecessor job connected by a trigger edge compared to all other methods.

The proposed method sometimes lost to other methods when the number of cores in a cluster is small and the number of nodes is large ((b), (c), (d), (h), and (l) of Fig. 6, especially when $cluster\_num=20$ ). This is considered to be due to the effect of Comb_fit. In the average task set, each job requires 1–9 cores, and in $cluster\_num=20$ of Fig. 6, the number of required cores is most likely to exceed the number of cores in a cluster. In the proposed method, Comb_fit is considered to be called more often. At this time, the pattern (d) has the largest number of clusters and the number of cores in a single cluster is 1–4, which increases the likelihood of finding a combination by Comb_fit. However, the selection of clusters by Comb_fit results in a single node irregularly selecting clusters from various locations. Other methods have a certain pattern in cluster selection. In AIS, clusters with a smaller index are selected preferentially, and there is a higher probability that nodes connected by a trigger edge use the same cluster. In addition, when selecting multiple clusters, in Best_fit and Greedy_fit, the clusters are similarly checked from the smallest index clusters. Therefore, it can be assumed that the clusters with smaller index are more likely to be used more often and hence nodes connected by a trigger edge are more likely to be allocated to the same clusters than the proposed method. Although the proposed method uses Pred_fit, we consider that it is more difficult to find clusters that satisfy the requirements (Line 8 in Algorithm 2), because the remaining cores of each cluster are small in case of $cluster\_num=20$ . Therefore, compared to the other methods, a job secures cores from various clusters, resulting in more clusters that are different from each other connected by a trigger edge. However, Comb_fit is able to use up the few remaining clusters and keep the clusters with a large remainder of cores. In other words, the clusters used are more distributed, but they are effective in reducing inter-cluster communication within a node.

The reason why AIS performs better after the proposed method is that the selection tends to be concentrated on some clusters with small indices; Greedy_fit and Best_fit also prioritize small index clusters, but these methods prioritize the number of remaining cores over the cluster index, and the selections of clusters are more likely to be scattered than in AIS. Hence, we consider AIS to be the next most reduced of the proposed methods.

Next, we compare PT-WCM and T-WCM. PT-WCM is able to reduce inter-cluster communication between nodes better than T-WCM. The difference is found to decrease as the number of clusters increases. This is similar to the discussion of Basic Methods, and is thought to be due to the fact that the disadvantage of Comb_fit becomes larger and cluster selection by Pred_fit becomes more difficult as the number of clusters increases. However, under all cluster architectures, PT-WCM is able to produce good results.

Next, in the comparison between PN-WCM and N-WCM, unlike Fig. 5, bfPN-WCM is able to reduce inter-cluster communication between nodes significantly more than N-WCM. We believe that this is because Pred_fit worked very well, as almost all nodes will require one core.

sec.title: Comparison of Average Maximum Response Time in Fig. 7
sec.p:
The changes in the average maximum response time when $cc\_cost$ is varied as shown in Fig. 7. Here, the evaluation is carried out with the number of nodes set to 80. First, Basic Methods are discussed. The results show that the proposed method is able to reduce the average maximum response time in all cluster architectures. This is due to the fact that the proposed method reduces the inter-cluster communication both within a node and between nodes, although the proposed method loses to other methods in (b), (c), (d), and (h) of Fig. 6 when the number of node is 80, as it reduces the inter-cluster communication within a node, proposed method is most successful in reducing the impact of inter-cluster communication in these patterns of Fig. 7. FIGURE 7.
Comparison of the average maximum response time when varying the number of $cc\_cost$ in average task set.Number of nodes is 80.

In (a), (e) and (i) of Fig. 5, the proposed method loses slightly when the number of nodes is small compared to Best_fit. However, it is clear from Fig. 7 that the difference between the proposed method and Best_fit is very large when $cluster\_num=5$ . In addition, the difference between the proposed method and Best_fit is very small in Fig. 5, and it can be concluded that the proposed method is superior to the Best_fit.

Next, we compare PT-WCM and T-WCM. Figs. 5 and 6 show that PT-WCM has lower inter-cluster communication compared to Basic Methods. Overall, however, the response time is greater than Basic Methods. This is because the allocation by WCM resulted in generating more nodes requiring nine cores compared to the case of random require (Basic Methods); requiring nine cores is a fairly large core request, and more nodes are expected to wait for nine cores to become available as the number of parallel jobs increases. Therefore, the delay due to waiting time is expected to increase somewhat. Another factor is that the number of nodes that can benefit from parallel processing will decrease because the number of nodes requiring one core will also increase. If the value of parallelism K is small, the execution time may not change much even if nine cores are allocated. On the other hand, nodes with a large degree of parallelism can significantly reduce execution time even with a small number of cores. When the value of $cc\_cost$ is increased, PT-WCM can reduce the response time more than Basic Methods in more cases. This indicates that depending on the time of one inter-cluster communication, the reduction of inter-cluster communication outweighs the impact of latency and execution time.

Next, a comparison of PN-WCM and N-WCM shows that PN-WCM is slightly better. We believe this is because the number of inter-cluster communication occurrences is lower, and thus the impact of this is less. Here, the response times for PN-WCM and N-WCM are significantly larger than for all the other methods. This is due to waiting for execution. In the absence of thresholds, WCM attracts cores to some nodes to an extreme degree, as described in Section IV-A2. Therefore, in the worst case scenario, a single node may request $total\_core\_num$ cores. This would take a great deal of time because execution would stop until all cores are available. Therefore, we consider that the average value of the maximum response time is large.

sec.label: F.
sec.title: Evaluation of the Heavy Task Set
Comparison of Inter-Cluster Communication Within A Node in Fig. 8
sec.p:
We investigated the heavy task set when the $heavy\_task\_num$ varied. This time, the number of nodes is fixed at 80. Fig. 8 shows the proposed method reduced inter-cluster communication within a node the most in the heavy task set. The overall results show that the occurrence of inter-cluster communication is reduced as the value of $heavy\_task\_num$ increases. Particularly striking examples are (a), (c), (e), (g), (i), and (k) in Fig. 8. Here, it can be seen that when $heavy\_task\_num = 5$ , the values of the proposed method drop sharply. From this, an interesting observation can be made. Let’s take (a), (c) and (i), which are $cluster\_num=5$ , as examples. When $heavy\_task\_num = 5$ , it means that five heavy tasks require $\frac {total\_core\_num}{heavy\_task\_num}$ cores, which is equal to the number of cores in one cluster in the five-cluster case. This means that when the heavy task requires cores, if any one cluster has all the cores left over, inter-cluster communication within a node will not occur. In the case of $heavy\_task\_num \leq 4$ , the number of required cores by the heavy tasks exceeds one cluster, and inter-cluster communication occurs every time a heavy task is executed. The same idea can be said for $cluster\_num=10$ . In this time, the heavy tasks require the number of cores in two clusters. In (a), (e), and (i), the same phenomenon can be observed for Best_fit. As mentioned in Section IV-E1, this is thought to be because Best_fit can allocate cores without using some clusters until the end. Therefore, when the number of required cores for one cluster arrives, the probability that one cluster can handle it in these cases is very high. However, the same phenomenon as the proposed method could not be confirmed for cases (c), (g), and (k). This is because Best_fit selects the largest number of clusters in situations where multiple clusters are selected. FIGURE 8.
Comparison of the average number of inter-cluster occurrences within a node in the heavy task set. The number of nodes is 80.

Comparing Best_fit and Greedy_fit, Best_fit performs better than Greedy_fit in situations where the total number of cores is low. Greedy_fit is better than or about the same as Best_fit for more total number of cores. The heavy task set makes a large core request with $heavy\_task\_num$ tasks generating inter-cluster communication. However, these tasks are few in number relative to the total number of nodes, mostly nodes require 1-3 cores. When a job comes in that can be handled by a single cluster, Greedy_fit chooses the cluster with the largest remainder. Therefore, the number of cores remaining in each cluster gradually decreases evenly. Therefore, only one or zero cores remain in each cluster, and when a job requiring three cores arrives, cores must be allocated from three clusters. This situation occurs more often than Best_fit. On the other hand, in the Best_fit method, the clusters are used from the smallest remainders, which leads to a large number of cores being easily left in some of the clusters until the end. However, since the number of heavy tasks is very small, there are only a few situations where Greedy_fit is advantageous. Furthermore, increasing the number of total cores does not change the number of tasks other than heavy task and the number of required cores by those nodes. Therefore, when the number of cores in a cluster is small, the disadvantage of Greedy_fit, that it is difficult to leave a large number of cores in some clusters, is easily affected, and Best_fit is more advantageous. The number of required cores does not change even if the number of total cores increases, except for heavy tasks. Therefore, it is thought that the disadvantage of Greedy_fit has less impact on the number of cores. Since the proposed method uses these methods differently depending on the situation, it is able to avoid the disadvantages of each method and make good use of its advantages.

Next, a comparison of PT-WCM and T-WCM showed that PT-WCM is able to significantly reduce inter-cluster communication within a node, similar to Fig. 5. A comparison of PN-WCM and N-WCM shows that PN-WCM slightly reduces inter-cluster communication within a node, as shown in Fig. 5. In the evaluation of PN-WCM and N-WCM in the heavy task set, since the number of nodes is fixed and no threshold is set, the number of required cores per $heavy\_task\_num$ did not change, and only the total number of cores changed slightly. Therefore, in PN-WCM and N-WCM, the number of inter-cluster communications does not change significantly when $heavy\_task\_num$ varied.

sec.title: Comparison of Inter-Cluster Communication Between Nodes in Fig. 9
sec.p:
The results of the average inter-node communication between nodes in the heavy task set are shown in Fig. 9. The proposed method has the lowest incidence of inter-cluster communication between nodes in all situations. We attribute this to the fact that jobs other than the heavy task set require 1–3 cores and are therefore more likely to select clusters by Pred_fit. In the average task set, all jobs require any of 1–9 cores, and it is more difficult to benefit from Pred_fit because the number of cores in a cluster is very small. FIGURE 9.
Comparison of the average number of inter-cluster occurrences between nodes in the heavy task set. The number of nodes is 80.

In the comparison between Best_fit and Greedy_fit, Greedy_fit has better results when the value of $heavy\_tasik\_num$ is small. On the other hand, when the number of $heavy\_tasik\_num$ is large, Best_fit is more favorable. When the value of $heavy\_task\_num$ is small, the value of required cores by the heavy task is very large. Therefore, Best_fit will select a very large number of clusters. This increases the probability of inter-cluster communication with the node following the heavy task. On the other hand, Greedy_fit can handle such a situation with a small number of clusters, thus reducing the probability of inter-cluster communication with the following node. As the value of $heavy\_tasik\_num$ increases, the disadvantage of Best_fit becomes smaller because the maximum number of clusters required by a heavy task decreases. In Greedy_fit, the clusters used by the nodes are easily distributed, not depending on the number of heavy tasks. Therefore, as the value of $heavy\_tasik\_num$ increases, the impact of the disadvantage of Best_fit becomes smaller, and the difference with Greedy_fit is expected to reverse.

In the AIS, as described in Section IV-E2, we consider that the degree of distribution of the clusters used is smaller than that of Best_fit and Greedy_fit, because the most jobs are concentrated in the clusters with the smallest index.

Next, in the comparison between PT-WCM and T-WCM, PT-WCM is able to significantly reduce inter-cluster communication between nodes. In the comparison between PN-WCM and N-WCM, due to the success of Pred_fit, as described in Section IV-E2, PN-WCM is able to reduce inter-cluster communication more.

sec.title: Comparison of Average Maximum Response Time in Fig. 10
sec.p:
The variation of the average maximum response time in the heavy task set with varying $cc\_cost$ is shown in Fig. 10. The number of nodes in the DAG is set to 80 and fixed at $heavy\_task\_num = 5$ for the evaluation. The reason for setting $heavy\_task\_num = 5$ is that in Fig. 8, the Best_fit has almost the same results as the proposed method when $cluster\_num=5$ . Firstly, (a), (e), and (i) in Fig. 10 show that the proposed method is able to suppress the average maximum response time for Best_fit. FIGURE 10.
Comparison of average maximum response times for varying $cc\_cost$ in the heavy task set. The number of DAGs is 80 and $heavy\_task\_num=5$ .

AIS generated the most inter-cluster communication within a node. On the other hand, AIS is able to reduce the occurrence of inter-cluster communication between nodes next to the proposed method. However, the response time results of AIS are the worst. This result shows that it is important to reduce inter-cluster communication both within a node and between nodes.

Next, a comparison of PT-WCM and T-WCM compared to the average task set opened a gap in response time over Basic Methods. This is due to the fact that the threshold value $\frac {total\_core\_num}{heavy\_task\_num}$ increased the number of cores allocated per node, resulting in an increase in latency for waiting, and that the number of nodes capable of parallel processing decreased as the number of nodes requiring one core increased. Overall, however, PT-WCM is able to significantly reduce response time compared to T-WCM. A comparison of PN-WCM and N-WCM shows that, similar to Section IV-E3, PN-WCM is able to reduce response time overall, although the difference is small.

sec.title: Analysis of the Proposed Method
sec.p: The proposed method is found to significantly reduce inter-cluster communication both within a node and between nodes in various cluster architectures. However, in some situations, the proposed method is outperformed by other methods.

In (b), (c), (d), (h), and (l) of Fig. 6, the proposed method lost to Basic Methods. These are slight disadvantages for reducing inter-cluster communication both within a node and between nodes; The losses of Fig. 6 are the disadvantages that arise from using Comb_fit to reduce inter-cluster communication within a node and a decrease in the opportunity to utilize Pred_fit due to the increase in the number of clusters.

However, these losses are very small compared to other methods. In fact, in the evaluations of the average maximum response time when considering the impact of inter-cluster communication both within a node and between nodes in Fig. 7, the proposed method has the smallest average maximum response time for all cluster architectures.

sec.title: Potential of the Proposed Method
sec.p: The proposed method is found to be highly effective in reducing inter-cluster communication both within a node and between nodes, irrespective of the cluster structure. This suggests that the proposed method can achieve very high performance when used on, for example, Kalray Coolidge MPPA 3-80 [23] with five clusters and 80 cores, or on P870-D [20], a RISC-V based clustered many-core processor, with up to 64 clusters and 256 cores in total. It is also found to perform well in task sets with jobs that require an extremely large number of cores, such as the heavy task set. This leads us to believe that the proposed method is also useful for running real applications, such as NDT scan matching [22] in Autoware or deep learning workloads [23], using clustered many-core processors.

Although our scheduler was evaluated solely on homogeneous many-core processors in this study, it could in principle be extended to systems that combine CPUs and GPUs such as NVIDIA DRIVE AGX Orin and Thor. In such an extension, each GPU Streaming Multiprocessor (SM) would be modeled as an individual cluster node, and DAG nodes could be assigned at the level of CUDA kernels or thread blocks. Important considerations include incorporating host to device DMA latencies and memory bandwidth contention between SMs into the cost model, as well as handling GPU kernels that cannot be interrupted by limiting concurrent launches and employing multiple CUDA streams to simulate time slicing. While these modifications suggest that our real-time guarantees may still be maintained, accurately modeling warp scheduling behavior within each SM, synchronization cost, and effective overlap of CUDA streams remain open challenges for future work.

sec.title: Scalability of the Proposed Method
sec.p: Through extensive simulation across 12 diverse cluster architectures (ranging from 5 to 20 clusters and 80 to 160 total cores), the proposed scheduler consistently reduced inter-cluster communication within nodes, and in most configurations, also between dependent nodes (Figs. 5 and 6). Although its advantage slightly diminishes when using a large number of very small clusters, its communication-aware cluster selection policy leads to more compact mappings that minimize inter-node and intra-node data transfers. Furthermore, as shown in Figs. 7 and 10, the average maximum response time tends to increase proportionally with the communication-to-computation cost ratio, indicating a predictable latency trend. In heavy-task scenarios (e.g., $heavy\_task\_num \geq 5$ ), the scheduler preferentially maps demanding nodes to entire clusters, effectively suppressing inter-node transfers and yielding lower latency even under high load (Fig. 9). These findings validate that careful modeling of communication overhead, combined with topology-aware dynamic cluster selection, provides a scalable foundation for deploying real-time DAG workloads on clustered many-core processors. While real hardware validation and memory contention modeling remain future work, the proposed method has shown its robustness and adaptability across various system sizes and workloads, including autonomous driving DAGs.
